comments.author: jimmytucson
comments.why_zh: Hettinger 解释了为什么 for-else 本该叫 nobreak。
comments.quote_zh: 他说，如果他有台时光机，他就能告诉未来的 Guido：我们现在都在用结构化编程了
comments.text_zh: 原因在这里（Hettinger）：> 1991 年时，“else”是显而易见的选择，因为编译器传统上就是这么实现 while 循环的：pastebin.com/tY35CTJ4 也就是说，“如果我还没跑完这个循环，就 GOTO 循环体”。他说，如果他有台时光机，他就能告诉未来的 Guido：我们现在都在用结构化编程了，所以没人会觉得“else”直观；不如叫它“nobreak”：[VIDEO] Guido 说，如果他有台时光机，他压根就不会把这个特性加进去：[LINK] 这整件事是 Knuth 的主意，不是 Guido 的：[LINK]
comments.text: Here’s why (Hettinger): > In 1991, “else” was the obvious choice because of the traditional way compilers implemented while-loops: pastebin.com/tY35CTJ4 That is, “if I haven’t finished the loop, GOTO the body.” He says if he had a time machine he could tell Guido in the future we’re all using structured programming so no one will find “else” intuitive; call it “nobreak” instead: [VIDEO] Guido says if he had a time machine he would not have included the feature at all: [LINK] This whole thing was Knuth’s idea, not Guido’s: [LINK]

comments.author: greggyb
comments.story_title: A Python Guide for the Ages
comments.why_zh: Hettinger 将 for-else 追溯到 Knuth 和 goto，并建议把它命名为 nobreak。
comments.text_zh: Raymond Hettinger 对此有很好的讲解，把它追溯到 Knuth 关于在 'goto' 面前的结构化编程的论述。他建议把这个关键字叫作 'nobreak'，而不是 'else'。任何循环内部都有一个条件判断和一个跳转。用伪代码来说：if not <循环结束条件> then <执行循环体内容> <跳转到循环顶部> else //循环已完成 <在循环自然终止的情况下执行的内容> 如果我们因为某种原因在循环体里 'break'，我们就永远不会执行到这代码块里的 'else'。正如 Hettinger 先生解释的那样，对于任何读过 Knuth 或来自 'goto' 式控制流背景的人来说，这一点很明显。这不是侮辱，而是观察。（不）幸的是，结构化编程现在是绝对的主流规范，我们直接学习循环结构，而不是先学 'goto' 再逐步构建出循环结构。尤其是在像 Python 这样拥有丰富迭代协议的语言里，循环结构其实是 'goto' 的花哨包装这一点就非常不明显了。演讲链接：[VIDEO]
comments.text: Raymond Hettinger has a good section on this, tracing it back Knuth's discourse on structured programming in the face of 'goto'. He suggests calling the keyword 'nobreak', rather than 'else'. Inside any loop are a conditional and a jump. In pseudocode: if not <loop end condition> then <do loop things> <jump to top of loop> else //loop is done <do things in the case that the loop has terminated naturally> If we 'break' in the body of the loop for some reason, we will never hit the 'else' in this chunk of code. As Mr. Hettinger explains, this is obvious to anyone reading Knuth or coming from a 'goto' style of control flow. This is not an insult, but an observation. (Un)Fortunately, structured programming is the absolute norm now, and we learn looping constructs directly, rather than learning 'goto' and then building to looping constructs. Especially in a language with rich iteration protocols, such as Python, it is very much unapparent that the looping constructs are fancy wrappers around 'goto'. Link to the talk: [VIDEO]
